newsitem.title: USA: Princess Diana's best dresses to be auctioned off.
newsitem.headline: Princess Diana's best dresses to be auctioned off.

text.p: Next week, anyone can pretend to be a princess -- for a price.

Famed auction house Christie's is selling 79 of Princess Diana's elegant dresses and gowns, with the proceeds to go to AIDS and cancer research. Christie's executives have given the sale the slogan "Sequins save lives."

To committed Di-watchers, many dresses will be familiar. There is the pink-and-white, off-the-shoulder satin ball gown she wore in Berlin and a V-necked, midnight-blue sheath she wore to a fashion designer's gala in New York two years ago.
The selection also includes a handful of items Diana only wore privately that are making their first public appearance.

Selling the dresses for charity is an idea attributed to Diana's son Prince William. But the princess had another reason many people will readily understand, said Christie's creative marketing director Meredith Etherington-Smith, who visited Diana at Kensington Palace.
"She had no more room," Etherington-Smith said. "If you had a closet full of clothes, what would you do? Sell them."

The hardest dress for Diana to part with, she said, was a strapless, beaded oyster satin gown with a bolero jacket that she wore to a state banquet in Paris in 1988. The dress graces the cover of the auction catalogue, on sale for $50.
"She yo-yoed a bit about it," Etherington-Smith said. "It was in the sale, then she took it out. Then she said we must sell it."

Professional royals-watcher Richard Mineards, on hand for a press preview on Wednesday ahead of the June 25 sale, said he saw three types of buyers for Di's dresses. First are institutions and museums that could add a dress to their collections, and second are "ladies who lunch" who would love to boast about owning such a dress, he said.
The third are drag queens. "That's got to be the most amusing."

Interest in the sale has been high, Christie's said. It could easily rival the frenzy over last year's sale at Sotheby's of Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis' belongings, which fetched more than $34 million.
Christie's will not make an official guess as to the success of its sale. Bidding on each dress starts at $5,000.

"We have no reference point. It's not like looking up the last price of a Rembrandt," Etherington-Smith said. "But I expect packed and hysterical salesrooms, phones ringing off the hook and auction books groaning with bids."
The auction room holds 1,100 people, selected through a lottery. Diana will not be one of them, but she will attend a fund-raising dinner two days earlier, Christie's said.
"We never like to have the client at an auction," Etherington-Smith said. "It can be quite painful, and we don't want someone crying in the middle of the salesroom."
The gowns date over 15 years, showing Diana's taste evolving from frills and beadwork to more simple elegance.
The dress most likely to realise the highest bid, Mineards guessed, will be a midnight-blue velvet dress Diana wore to a White House dinner, when she danced with actor John Travolta.
